title: The meal chant
hook: the reflection before eating: this food is for health, not for vanity

segments.voice: Yesterday, remembering the dead: the home altar, the yearly rite, Maudgalyayana and his mother. Your line was they are remembered. Did you say someone's name out loud? Day one thousand four hundred ten.

Lunch at a monastery. The bowls are full, the food is warm, and everyone is hungry. Nobody starts eating. Instead, the monks chant a few lines together, in Pali, quietly, before the first bite. In a Zen hall the same pause happens with different words and wooden clappers. To a guest it can look strange, sitting in front of good food and not eating it yet. But the pause is the point. What are they saying in those few lines? Mostly, they are reminding themselves what eating is for. Today, the meal chant.
screen: `FULL BOWLS, NOBODY EATING YET.` → `A FEW LINES CHANTED FIRST.` → `WHAT IS EATING FOR?`

segments.voice: One source is in the Middle Length Discourses, in a teaching on how to let go of what clouds the mind. One of the ways is wise use, and food is one of the things used. The Buddha says a monk reflects wisely as he eats: not for fun, not for intoxication, not for putting on bulk, not for looking good. Only to keep this body going, to ease the pangs of hunger, and to support the holy life. That's the thought behind today's line. For health, not vanity. In Theravada monasteries, a form of these words is still chanted at meals. Notice how unfussy it is. It doesn't say food is bad, or the body is shameful, or eating is a sin. It says eat. Just know why. Hunger is real, and food meets it. But food can also be pulled into other jobs: showing off, numbing out, comforting yourself after a bad day, turning a meal into a contest. The reflection doesn't scold any of that. It quietly puts food back in its place. Zen communities have their own meal verses, which turn the same idea in another direction: considering the work that brought this food, and receiving it to support the practice. And then there's the pause itself. Before the first bite, there is one breath where you know what you are doing. For the Buddha, eating wisely was one way of guarding the mind. A bowl of rice becomes a small practice at every meal, already built into your life.
screen: `WISE USE OF FOOD.` · `NOT FOR FUN, NOT FOR LOOKS.` · `TO KEEP THE BODY GOING.` · then, large: `ONE BREATH BEFORE THE FIRST BITE.`

segments.voice: Sit for a moment, if you'd like, and notice whether you're hungry right now. Just notice; no need to change it. Then let the next meal come to mind, whenever it will be. See yourself sitting down in front of it. Before you pick anything up, you could say a short reflection drawn from the Buddha's words, quietly or in your head: not for fun, not for looks, only to keep this body going. Try saying it now, once, slowly. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The meal chant. The reflection before eating: this food is to keep the body going and support the practice, not for fun or looks. Today's word.
Your line: for health, not vanity. At your next meal, take one breath before the first bite, and remember what the food is for. Day one thousand four hundred ten.

howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries, monks recite a reflection on the purpose of food before eating, drawn from the Buddha's teaching on wise use; Zen communities chant their own meal verses before formal meals.

original.note: Pali patisankha: reflecting wisely, the word the meal reflection begins with.

trapdoor: what you thought: a grace before meals is about thanks.
what it means: the meal chant reminds the eater what food is for: health and practice, not vanity.
what a scholar hears: the Sabbasava Sutta's wise use of almsfood, recited at Theravada meals, and Zen's own meal verses.

sources.ref: Sabbasava Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 2), on wise use

notes: MN 2 paraphrased: 'reflecting wisely, he uses almsfood, not for amusement, intoxication, bulk or beautification, but only for the endurance and continuance of this body, for ending discomfort, for assisting the holy life'. Confirm the paraphrase.
The practice line ('not for fun, not for looks, only to keep this body going') is a paraphrase of MN 2, offered as a reflection, not a new prayer. Confirm this is acceptable.
Zen meal verses described only generally (the work that brought the food, receiving it to support practice); confirm.
Theravada chanting of the patisankha reflection at meals described generally; confirm.
Original: Pali patisankha in Devanagari; confirm spelling and pronunciation.

Editor: cut the unsourced superlative 'the oldest version'; hook no longer tells the listener what they feel; replaced the production word 'carry'; fixed 'comforting a bad day'; removed a doubled bell line in the practice.
